page.text:
This distinction between free and bound variables is entirely analogous
to familiar constructs in calculus and linear algebra: the index $i$ in a
sum $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i$ or the variable $t$ in a definite integral
$\int_a^b f(t)\,dt$ is bound, while $n$, $a$, and $b$ are free. Renaming
$t$ to $u$ in $\int_a^b f(u)\,du$ leaves the integral unchanged (a
property known in logic as *$\alpha$-equivalence*).

Care is required when substituting expressions into formulas: if a
substituted term contains a variable that happens to match a quantifier
inside the formula, accidental *variable capture* can occur, radically
corrupting the meaning. A rigorous deductive system systematically
renames bound variables whenever substitution threatens to capture them.
